utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I say at the outset that in the absence of Judge Van Den Wyngaert, Judge David and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis, and may I also apologise for the late start. I'm afraid that the other functions that I have got in the way, and I apologise for that. Are we able to start now, or do you have a point to make, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly. On Thursday last week, the Prosecution made a submission calling the Trial Chamber's attention to Rule 67(A)(2) of the rules which obliges the Defence to disclose any statements of Defence witnesses prior to the commencement of the Defence case. The Prosecution informed the Chamber that it has thus far received only 12 statements of Defence witnesses. At that time, the Chamber invited the Prosecution to bring to the Chamber's attention additional jurisprudence on the issue, particularly from the ad hoc tribunals. The Prosecution wishes to make a brief submission clarifying its understanding of the jurisprudence with respect to how the term "witness statement" has been defined by the relevant decisions and to renew its request to the Defence to produce those documents properly considered witness statements under the law. According to the jurisprudence, a witness statement is to be interpreted as "the account of a person's knowledge of a crime which is recorded through due procedure in the course of an investigation into the crime." This definition was set out in the Blaskic case by the Appeals Chamber in its decision on the appellant's motions for the production of material, suspension, or extension of the briefing schedule and additional filings. That decision was entered on the 26th of December, 2000, and the cite that I mentioned is from paragraph 15. This jurisprudence was cited by this very Trial Chamber in its 3rd of November, 2008, decision on the Defence motion to bar testimony of Zehra Turjacanin in paragraph 12. In that decision, this Trial Chamber stated - and this was with respect to a document that was entitled "interview notes" - that the Chamber stated that due to the fact that the notes "record Zehra Turjacanin's recollections regarding events in Bikavac that relate to charges in the indictment..." and it goes on - that's the only relevant portion, closed quote - they clearly fall within the meaning of witness statement. The fact that a particular witness statement does not correspond to a particular standard or form does not relieve a party from its obligation to disclose, and for that proposition I would cite the Appeals Chamber in the -- in an ICTR case entitled the Niyitegeka judgement, entered on the 9th of July, 2004, at paragraph 31. Therefore, the Prosecution submits that according to the jurisprudence of the ad hoc tribunals, ICTY and ICTR, and the law of this case as articulated by this Trial Chamber, any statement or declaration made by a witness in relation to an event he or she witnessed related to this case, regardless of the form it was recorded and regardless of who recorded it, falls within the meaning of a witness statement, whether that person who recorded it is an investigator, an attorney, or a translator. Last week, Mr. Cole also cited the Brima and the Norman cases from the special court for Sierra Leone. We support this proposition. I will not repeat those cites at this time. The jurisprudence recognises that work product or internal notes which fall under Rule 70(A) or not disclosable, but the fact that a document contains such material does not relieve a party from disclosing the material contained in the document which is properly disclosable. Redactions can be made to those portions of the document which contain material protected by Rule 70(A). We have received no disclosure for the next witness, and I would ask Mr. Alarid to provide me with any prior statements of the witness as that term is defined by the jurisprudence or confirm on the record that the Milan Lukic Defence team is not in possession of such. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we need to hear any further comments. I was saying I don't think we need to hear any further comments on that. It's a statement of the Prosecution's idea as to what the law is on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I would only ask if the Trial Chamber is going to consider that submission and make a ruling on it, we would like to have the opportunity to respond in writing, and in which case we would ask for the citations that were cited by Mr. Cole the other day to be provided to us in some form that we can actually track down the cases, as we do not have access to the Prosecution's digest that was cited to -- by Mr. Cole in the last court session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, if -- if the matter arises in a practical way, then of course I'll deal with it. But the Rule itself is quite clear, Mr. Ivetic, that if you have the statements, then you must produce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, as I have said, I believe this is now the third or fourth time I'm saying this, we have provided the statements from witnesses that we have in our possession. As far as I'm aware, we've disclosed them all. I don't have a list prepared because I did not anticipate that we were going to be going forward with this topic, but we've given them everything, and then pursuant to the rules we've given them a summary for the viva voce witnesses of what that witness -- what topics that witness is supposed to testify about, and that's -- we feel that we've complied with the rules, Your Honour. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The only way it would arise in a practical way is if you have refrained from providing something which qualifies as a witness statement according to the case law that Mr. Groome has just outlined, and in which case, then, I would have to rule on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour, but then we'd also have the right to give submissions as to what qualifies as a statement or not. I can tell you as I've told you with respect to the witness that we had here last week, I met with this witness. I met -- with the first witness that's coming in, I met with her the first time approximately four -- four or five weeks ago when I went out into the terrain, and then I met with her this morning. I've been trying to find out about the case, and in that process I ask questions. That's what every attorney does. I've been in this Tribunal for now almost ten years, and this procedure by the Prosecution from these special ad hoc tribunals is something that I've seen practiced nowhere in this Tribunal in the way that is being offered by the Prosecution. I mean, my preparation to present -- are they entitled to have my questions that I've prepared to ask this witness? I mean, that's -- it seems to be remarkable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we're not arguing that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is that if you have something which might qualify if one were to accept Mr. Groome's submissions, then if you are to discharge your duties as an officer of the court properly, you must bring that to our attention, and the Chamber will make a ruling on the matter. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge with respect to these two witnesses, everything has been provided that would fall under that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Let's have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness -- the first witness, Your Honour, is Mrs. Anka Vasiljevic testifying without protective measures and viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe she's the fifth witness, Your Honour. We have the one that did not complete the cross-examination. It's still open. And including that individual, we have had four witnesses who have testified here. So this would be our fifth -- fifth witness in sequence. Sixth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll check on that later, but let the witness make the declaration in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit and you may begin. The registrar says she's the fifth witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that correction, Your Honour. WITNESS: ANKA VASILJEVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam. I'll wait for the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I trust you can hear me now with your headphones on. As you know, I'm one of the attorneys for Milan Lukic in this case, and this afternoon I would have some questions for you. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I would ask that you start by first stating your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anka Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could tell us where it is, that is to say, what city and what country do you presently reside in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Visegrad in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm waiting for the transcript to catch up. I apologise. I have to wait for the translation and the transcript to catch up with us even though I can understand what you're saying since I have one ear available. And where is it that you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Valjevo, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when was it that you actually moved to the Visegrad municipality? What were the circumstances around that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got married in 1975, and when I graduated from university, as my husband came from Visegrad, in 1989 we both got jobs in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned your husband. Could you identify for us what the name of your husband was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Radomir Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, he is -- he is deceased? He is no longer with us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I -- was he also known by any other shortened versions of his -- of his name, first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called him Rasa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- now, if you could tell us a little bit about your late husband, Dr. Radomir Vasiljevic. First of all, what kind of man was he if you would have to describe him to us? What characteristics did he have or exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a great man, a great expert, a famous doctor, a good father, a good husband, a good friend. I can say only all the best about him. Nobody ever spoke ill of him. It's rare that such a person is born.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that he was a doctor. With respect to his education and training, was he a specific type of doctor? If you could explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was special. He was a specialist and epidemiologist, and he was a specialist in sports medicine, and he sub-specialised in AIDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you would just repeat the first speciality he had. It appears it did not make it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Epidemiologist, specialist in epidemics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, I'm just waiting for the transcript. And with respect to yourself, you indicated that you had finished some schooling before moving to Visegrad municipality. What schooling did you yourself accomplish and complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished school for commercial affairs, and I worked in a company for several years until it went bankrupt, in a commercial company.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if you could focus on the time-period of 1992, and when I say 1992, I include the time-period when there was a -- a war on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the former SFRY Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. During that time, did your late husband, Dr. Vasiljevic, was he employed as a doctor and, if so, where was he employed? So please give us the pre-war period and the -- during the war, if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, he worked in a work medicine health centre, and then until his death he was the director of the health care centre in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to that position as the director of the health centre in Visegrad, did he have occasion during that specific time-period, that is, before the war and during the war, to have a practice involving the treatment of actual patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you, madam, have any knowledge of whether Dr. Vasiljevic's practice of medicine before the war - now we're talking about just before the war - included the treatment of patients from Visegrad of different ethno-religious groups, and if so, what groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never paid attention to ethnicity. It was irrelevant. It was unimportant. We all got on well, socialised, and in his job especially, no distinctions could be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to your -- your husband's work as a doctor and as director of the health centre in Visegrad, were there -- before the war, were there personnel working with him in the health centre of differing ethnic or religious affiliations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We got on really well together. We were even on visiting terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to -- sorry, again, I had to wait for the transcript. Would you be able to identify any such individuals who were your household friends as you identified who were of a differing ethnic or religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a lot of names. Avdija Zahiragic; Alma and her husband, also a Muslim, I don't recall their last name; Dzevad Avdic; Hazim Ustamujic; Enver Jamak, and if need be, I can enumerate more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that would -- that would suffice. Did yourself or your husband treat these people differently, that is to say, did -- did you regard these people differently than your Serb friends, or could you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We all socialised together. We celebrated together. We Serbs have a holiday called slava. They would come to visit us, and they celebrated Bajram, so we visited then. We had barbecues together. We went on trips together. Our children went to school together. That sort of thing didn't happen in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, I'd like to turn to another topic, namely Mr. Milan Lukic. How long is it that you have known Mr. Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've known him since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what is the precise nature of your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him very well. We have the kum relationship. Among us Orthodox Serbs, there is this traditional relationship. He was my son's godfather at my son's christening, and when my son gets married he will be his best man.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to Mr. Milan Lukic, did you have occasion to see him in 1992 during the time-period of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. He went to visit -- came to visit us all the time in our home.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And before we get to those household visits, did you have occasion to see him out and about in the -- in the town during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes. We would run into each other in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to those encounters now, let's focus on the ones out in the street with Milan Lukic. What, if anything, could you tell us about those encounters? Who was he with? How was he attired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was war-time. Everybody wore a uniform. All men wore uniforms at that time, even my husband who was a doctor. No one wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And specifically with respect to Milan Lukic, did you ever encounter him on the streets in the company of other persons whom you recognised or knew from Visegrad, and if so, whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to see him. Our neighbour Dragan Tomic, who was a police commander, was often with him. Whether he was his driver or what, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- now, if we could focus for a time-period on the house visits when you said that Mr. Lukic came to visit you. Do you have an approximation as to how frequently that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how often, how frequently, but two times a month or once a month, but we did keep in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, I don't believe that we have covered exactly where you lived during 1992, during the war in Visegrad. Could you describe for us what neighbourhood you -- you lived in at that point in time or otherwise identify the location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We lived in a family house in a neighbourhood called Kalate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say "we lived," who else lived there with you, or who were the members of your family, of your immediate family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I have only my children left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the children living with you the entire time at the family home in the Kalate neighbourhood during 1992, during the hostilities in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Very often, they were staying with my parents in Valjevo. It was pointless to have one's children staying in Visegrad. Whoever could take their children somewhere else did so. Muslims -- the Muslims often shelled civilian facilities, schools, houses. They didn't select their targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get more to that time-period and to those occurrences later. With respect to that neighbourhood, you had indicated earlier -- let me just double-check the -- the reference.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone, the interpreters kindly request.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated your neighbour being a Dragan Tomic. Do you describe for us where or how close that house was of Mr. Tomic to the Vasiljevic family home where you resided with your husband during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the fourth house from ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, let's focus briefly for the time-period after the war. How often did you have occasion to encounter Milan Lukic after the war, and what can you tell us about those specific encounters with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would meet at slava celebrations. He would always come to our slava, and we would visit him when he had his slava. His family celebrates St. John's Day, which is a day after our slava. When his wife gave birth, we came to visit. When they baptised their little girl, we went to the christening. My family had many obligations, unfortunately, especially my husband, so we didn't have much time for a lot of socialising, but now I regret this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are slava celebrations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's something that exists only among Orthodox Serbs in Yugoslavia. It doesn't exist among the Greeks or the Russians. It's a saint's day. For example, my slava is St. George's Day, and on that day we celebrate that saint. He is the patron saint of my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every family has its own patron saint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the war, did Milan Lukic ever have occasion to assist you in regards to any requests relative to your husband or to your children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once when I came from work, I couldn't find my son. I was afraid. He was in the third grade of primary school at the time. As I had seen our kum with the police, I asked him to take a car and to look for my son. I thought he might have set out to his grandmother's by bus, so I asked him to go and look at that bus, but my son was at home. He was hiding. He had been frightened by something, and he was hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say: "I had seen our kum with the police, and I asked him to take a car..." who is that particular kum whom you made this request of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you asked him to take a car and look for the son. Do you know whether in fact he had complied with that request, and if so, how he undertook it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was frightened, and he immediately set out to look for him. He was in a panic, just as I was, and fortunately, everything ended well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it an ordinary type of car that he utilised, or was there anything special about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a police car. I had my own car, but I didn't think of asking him to drive my car because I was in a panic. So I think he used his official car.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion during the war to hear anything in Visegrad, any kind of gossip, rumours, or reports about Milan Lukic during the war and his -- and his activities during the war, and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. I didn't hear anything unusual compared to what I heard about other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. During the war, did you hear anything about any -- did you hear any bad things about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection as to leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say you didn't "hear anything unusual compared to what I heard about other men." What sorts of things did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was war-time. Everybody had been mobilised. Everybody went to war, and the only thing that was interesting was who would remain alive and who would be brought home dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've described all these various encounters with Milan during the war, either on the street or when he visited your familial home. How would you describe Mr. Milan Lukic's demeanour during those encounters that you had with him, again, during the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were very warm encounters. He loved my children. He loved all children. I heard that he gave sweets and chocolate to other children in our street, not to just my children. He liked joking around. He would encourage us, try to keep our spirits up if we were short of food or the Muslims were attacking. He would say, Hold on; just hang on; everything will be all right; this will all come to an end. He gave us moral support. He would say, Everything will be all right. And he adored children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, how, if you had to, would you describe his demeanour after the war? Did it differ in any regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. He had his own children then, and he was even more caring then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now based upon all these encounters with him, based upon your personal knowledge of Milan Lukic and your direct interactions with him, what opinion could you give us as to his character and personality in total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you everything. He was a good man, a good friend, a good comrade, a good kum. I can only say the best about him, all the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to have knowledge of his acts towards others, of him helping anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was very correct towards everyone. Everyone adored him in the town, and all the children loved him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about his interactions with adults? Did you have any occasion to become familiar with any specific instances as to his relations with adults either during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never in all these years, either in the course of the war or after the war did I hear anybody say a bad word about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anyone say anything positive about him, in particular that he had assisted them in any -- in any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He helped everybody, whoever asked for help. I had occasion to ask for his help only once, and he helped me. But whoever came to him for help, if he was able to help, he helped everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, did you have occasion at some point in time to become familiar with certain allegations of crimes against Milan Lukic, and if so, when and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned this when I found an indictment against Milan and Sredoje Lukic on the internet. I was shocked and surprised to see that. It was the first time I had heard about all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say you found an indictment against Milan and Sredoje, before what court was that indictment that we -- that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that you were surprised to see it and it was the first time that you heard about those things. Let me ask you specifically. During the war, did you have occasion as a resident of Visegrad to hear anything about any alleged instance of house-burnings wherein large numbers of persons of Muslim ethnicity perished and were killed in either the Pionirska or the Bikavac neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly never heard anything about that. Visegrad is a small town. News like that would have spread. If so many people had been burned alive, there would have been a stench that could simply not be concealed. It would have spread throughout the entire valley. This wasn't something that one could possibly have concealed. I think this is all a huge - what shall I call it - mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say it could not be concealed. It would have -- strike that. You say it's a small town. Do you have familiarity with any of the -- of those two sites that are alleged -- where it is alleged that this -- that this occurred? How familiar are you with those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said Visegrad is a small town. I know all of the places. I know about this one house. I'm not sure about the other, but I do know the other one. I live right next to it, as a matter of fact, the house where these people are alleged to have been burned alive. That particular house did burn down, but it certainly wasn't alone. Many Serb and Muslim houses burned down at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to what you found out when you examined the indictment in this case against Mr. Milan Lukic, are you able to reconcile any of those alleged acts contained therein with your personal knowledge and experience of Milan Lukic, the human being and person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with him. No way could I reconcile the two, and I really hope that everyone will see for themselves that this is simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One other individual I'd like to just ask you briefly about. Are you familiar with Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He's my husband's relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know him well enough to be able to describe him or tell us anything about him that stands out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him really well. He lived in our neighbourhood as well. We socialised before the war and later. He was an alcoholic. It is an embarrassing thing to say, but he was some sort of a clown or a buffoon around town. Everyone was having jokes at his expense. He was all right for everybody else but not for the own family or for his children. He was the laughingstock of the entire town.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Oh, I'm sorry. Go ahead, finish. I didn't realise you weren't finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite frequently during the war, they would call me because they knew he was my husband's relative. He would get drunk, fall asleep out in the street. I would drive over, pick him up, take him home, saying, Mitar, don't bring shame on our family like this. He liked me and he would listen to me. He would follow my advice. He would just get up, get into the car, and drive home with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, ma'am, if we could return back to the one topic you had started upon and I said we'd touch earlier, and that is to say, with respect to the Vasiljevic familial home wherein you resided, you indicated your children weren't there the entire time. I'd like to first ask you, did you remain in Visegrad the entire year in 1992, or did you have occasion to move or relocate somewhere else for any reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1991, on the 28th of May specifically, I gave birth to a daughter. Twenty days after that, I had to flee Visegrad. I got into my car with my baby and with my son who was 10 years old at the time. There was also another neighbour of ours with her baby. We had to flee Visegrad because we had been receiving phone threats. I didn't have the courage to send my son to school anymore. We were receiving a great many threats from the Muslims. I went to Valjevo with the children and stayed there until September 1991, throughout that summer, after which I returned to Visegrad. I was on sick leave at the time. I wasn't actually working. In May, possibly April, I can't be sure about the date, I had to flee again with the children. The day I drove through the tunnel was blown up in Dobrun, I came across a Muslim barricade. Not a Muslim barricade. It was a barricade or a roadblock that was erected by the police, but at the time all the Serbs had been driven out of the police, force and only Muslims remain in the force. They put up those huge spiky obstacles right in the middle of the road. They stopped me --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They started rummaging through our belongings, but there were only diapers there. We had two babies with us. I said, Please don't. I stood up to them. They threw my documents on the ground and said, Be gone. And this is how you speak to a dog over where I come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One microphone at a time while the witness is speaking, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- if we can go back. You had indicated you were receiving threats and you did not have courage to send your son to school. Could you give us more details relating to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at night-time, 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning. They would phone us to say, You'll send your son over to school, will you, but will he be back? That is the question. That's what they said. Sometime in February 1992, I think, one of my husband's colleagues, Avdija Zahiragic, came to our home. This man is still alive. He lives in Sarajevo. He said that he was not allowed to go to work anymore because he had heard in a body of the SDA that they would arrest him. From February on until the Uzice Corps came into town, he hadn't shown up for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you said he was not allowed to go to work anymore because they would arrest him, who is the "he" and the "him" in that portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what she said? The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, will you please repeat what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] February 1992, a colleague of my husband's came to our home, Avdija Zahiragic, and told him he shouldn't go to work anymore or mustn't go to work anymore because he heard from some people, his own party, the SDA, that it was Rasa's turn to be arrested now. Throughout this time, he allowed him to remain on sick leave and issued him with appropriate documents so that he wouldn't have to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think the Judge was asking me, when you say Rasa, is that -- who is that? I think we had mentioned that earlier, but just for the record, who is Rasa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radomir, my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, does that address your question or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that adequately address your question, or can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you -- during the time periods when you left Visegrad, you indicated you left with your neighbour. Do you have any knowledge as to what other persons in Visegrad were doing, other -- other civilians like yourself, were doing during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All those who had somewhere to move their children to over in Serbia did just that, all of them. Those who had to stay behind and work were quite scared to have to do that. I was lucky to be able to remain on sick leave at the time. There were horrible things going on. In broad daylight, they would pull a car over, force a man or a woman from the car, leave the car, and then just beat them there, right there in the street. There were no police around to complain to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to return to Visegrad at any point in time for work or otherwise, and if so, could you tell us about that, when it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back in 1992, May 1992, when the Uzice Corps came to Visegrad. They -- they called me to respond to what we refer to as the work assignment. All of us went back, both Serbs and Muslims. Many Muslims had fled Visegrad with their children previously. We all worked together as if nothing at all was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at that point in time, you said you had to respond to what you referred to as a work assignment. Did you in fact go back to your employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus on that time-period, what was the condition of the town of Visegrad during that time-period? Did you note any damage or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back to Visegrad, I could hardly recognise the place. It had been largely destroyed. All the shops were smashed up. It was a horrifying sight. It had turned into a horror town, shards of glass all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can return to your husband's line of work in 1992. During the war, did he have occasion to speak to you regularly about persons that he was treating as patients or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite rarely, in fact, only when there was something exceptional. He had taken the oath of Hippocrates, and he stuck to that. We hardly ever discussed his business at home, and this cut both ways. But whenever there was something exceptionally noteworthy, we might have brought it up with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was there in fact an occasion where there was something exceptional that you recall your husband relaying to you about persons treated by him during the course of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the summer of 1992, and I don't remember the date or the month. It might have been June or July. He came home and told me that he had never before seen a woman like that with burns of the highest degree. Her arms were burned, her face, her hair. She had tried to light a cigarette by using a gas stove and then caught fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- if we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was horrified by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could break this down a bit. First of all, you indicated that this individual's arms were burned, her face, her hair. Did -- what about the rest of her body? Did your husband relate to you anything with respect to the condition of the rest of her body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rest was all right. She could walk, but she caught fire when she tried to light a cigarette by using this gas stove. We have a gas stove, too, back at our home, and that's how I light my cigarette very often when I run out of matches. She leaned into the flame, and then the gas burned her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to discover the name or identity of the person who had suffered such injuries in the manner described, either from your husband or from any other source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time who he was talking about. However - and I'm not sure what the year was - a friend of ours from Sarajevo sent us a book by Ibrahim Klunj, called "Testimony." It was then that we found out the woman's name was Zehra Turjacanin who expressed her gratitude to Dr. Rasa because he had saved her life and helped her a great deal. I read later on on the internet and in the press about her evidence here at the Tribunal and realised that she had changed her story, which struck me as entirely pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now with respect to this individual, you had indicated earlier the method in which she was injured. Did your husband relay to you the bases for his knowledge that she had injured herself trying to light a cigarette by using a stove -- a gas stove? Did he illuminate the bases for his knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do know about that. There was a nurse who was with him at the time, another neighbour of ours. She worked at the health centre, Slavica Pabic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Babic"]. The two of them were called by the command jointly. There was a command at Bikavac. It's Papic, not Babic. They didn't know who this was. They had no idea that this woman was of a different ethnicity. They just got into the ambulance, they went there to pick her up, and when they picked her up they told them that. They gave her the shots, the medicines, and drove her back home. I'm not sure who the house that she was driven back to belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm sorry, if we could just have the last name of the individual who had authored this book called "Svedocinje" [phoen] or "Testimony"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ibrahim Kljun. He used to work as a photographer in Visegrad before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that a friend from Sarajevo had sent that to you. What was the ethnic or religious affiliation of that particular friend who sent that book to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, Hazim Ustamujic. Ustamujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment so I can consult my notes. I think ... I apologise. I don't have it on my screen now, but did you indicate when -- what time-period this friend sent the book from Sarajevo? Was it during the war or after the war? Can you -- can you narrow down the time-period at all for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was just before the end of the war. It might have been 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and how did your husband react upon receiving that book and -- and reading of Ms. Turjacanin's thanks and praise of him for assisting her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was glad she thought of him, but he was shocked when he heard about her other story.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could back up for a moment to another topic, another individual. Are you familiar with Miljana Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. The prettiest girl in Visegrad. She was a doctor too. She was my kum's girlfriend.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say she was the girlfriend of your kum, again, I have to ask you to specify. Which kum are you talking about? Which specific kum is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated she was a doctor too. What was it -- what was it -- what was her speciality or employment? Where did she work, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was a GP. She worked at the health centre. She didn't specialise in any particular field. Back where I come from, when a doctor completes his studies they take another four years to specialise and yet another four years to sub-specialise, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to ever witness or be visited by Milan and Dr. Miljana, and if so, what can you tell us about those visits? How did he act, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in love. She was pretty. She was a stunning beauty. I don't think I'd ever seen a woman as pretty as her in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm waiting for the transcript again. Could you tell us what time-period this was that Mr. Milan Lukic and Dr. Miljana Krsmanovic were boyfriend/girlfriend? Could you tell us what time-period that took place in? When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't quite say, I'm afraid. I might go wrong. Was it 1993 or 1994? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about in reference to the -- to the war? Was it before, during, after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Vasiljevic, I thank you. At this time I have no further questions in direct examination. I may have some more in re-direct depending on how my colleague on the other side proceeds, but at this time, Mrs. Vasiljevic, I'd like to thank you and pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Witness, whether your husband was in the habit of discussing his patients with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just when there was something extreme. I know of other two cases like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Vasiljevic. My name is Dermot Groome, and I'm going to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Can I begin by asking you, what was your family name before you married into the Vasiljevic family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned a few times of -- of working and being on sick leave during different periods. Can I ask you the name of the -- the company that you -- that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: UPI. UPI Visegrad. U-p-i. It was a huge corporation headquartered in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what kind of work does UPI do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where is the -- the physical location of where you worked in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The administration building. The centre of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've -- you've told us a bit about this kumship relationship that you have with Milan Lukic. Is it also true that your family has a kumship relationship with Sredoje Lukic as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't found anything in direct examination related to my client and family relations to Sredoje Lukic's family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that prevents the question asked being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get in a bit detail exactly the extent of this kumship relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we should move on. Mr. Ivetic spent 50 minutes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the objection sustained, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What -- you've spoken about slavas and patron saints. What is the patron saint of the Lukic family? What is their slava?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: St. John. St. John's Day. As a matter of fact, it's tomorrow, the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm a little unclear as to when precisely in the summer of 1992 you were physically present in Visegrad. I take it that you -- you said you returned at some point in May of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to be more precise about when in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be specific about the date, but it can be checked. It was after the Uzice Corps had entered Visegrad. It was after that that we all went back and we were called back to work, both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you returned to Visegrad in May of 1992, did you remain there throughout the course of the summer, in June, July, and August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I went to visit my children very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that -- that you lived right next to one of the houses that's the subject of -- of this case. Which house, if you can be more specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't live there. I now live next to the house in question, since a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you said that you live in Kalate, is that -- you live in Kalate now or you lived there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Kalate in 1992. I now live in Pionirska Street, house number 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea about where Kalate neighbourhood is in relation to the Pionirska Street or the Mahala section of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pionirska is not called Mahala. Mahala is another street, not Pionirska Street, and Kalate is near the River Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Kalate, is it on the right bank or the left bank of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it north of the town centre or south of the town centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Down the Drina River towards Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's south of the town; is that correct? I saw you nod your head. We need a verbal answer to record you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying that anything that happened in Pionirska Street in 1992, you would not have been in a position to hear it or witness any part of it from where your house was located in the Kalate section of town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object as to the question being too vague. He says "anything." If he has a specific instance or occurrence, let him -- let him specify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to me the witness should be in a position to answer. Can you answer the question, Witness? Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. From my house, you can't see the house in Pionirska Street, but it's so close that I would have had to smell the stench. I would have had to hear shooting. I have had opportunity to see what it looks like when a house is burning. Tiles shatter, walls crack. You have to hear that. I couldn't have seen it because there was a low hill between, but I would have smelt the stench, and I would have heard the noise because the smell of people burning is terrible. It's a disaster. I would have had to smell something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know what day the Pionirska Street fire took place or, in your view, it's alleged to have taken place. Do you know what the date is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I learned that from you, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So during June of 1992, you have no recollection of seeing, hearing, or smelling anything which would indicate to you that a large number of people were burnt to death; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. One would have to know. Visegrad Grad is a small town. People would talk about it. People would talk about it. Somebody would mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I couldn't help but notice when you walked into the courtroom, you waved at Mr. Milan Lukic and gave him a big smile. Would it be correct to say that you still have deep affection for Milan Lukic, your kum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I adore him. I love him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is a saint. He's like a patron saint of my family. He was my son's godfather. That's not a small matter. My son will not be able to get married until he gives him his blessing and takes him to church as his best man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you would join in celebrations with the family of your kum. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In 1992, did you join together to celebrate Djurdjevdan Day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't celebrate Djurdjevdan together. Everyone celebrates in their own house and guests arrive. My kum was my guest at my Slavs, and we were his guests at his slava. As my husband was unable to go at the time, I went there with my son because this goes down the male line in the family. Women do not inherit the kum relationship; only men do. I went with my son so that my son could break the cake at his slava celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you remind me again, what is your slava?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: St. George. That's Djurdjevdan, on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did Milan Lukic come to your home to help celebrate Djurdjevdan Day with you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in 1992 but in 1993. I don't think I knew him then, but I did get to know him in 1993, and then he came regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the year that the child -- your child was born that he's the godfather?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it seems you first met Milan Lukic when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My child was born in 1982, but as Milan comes from a village near Visegrad, he went to school there, as I heard, and then he was away working somewhere on a temporary basis, so I didn't meet him, and it was only after 1987 that I began to live in Visegrad permanently. He was already away from Visegrad. I knew his parents, and I met him only when he came back in 1992, and he was my son's godfather on Djurdjevdan in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So did you -- when in 1992 did you meet Milan Lukic? Is it during the summer or after the summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992? Well, as soon as he arrived in Visegrad we got to know one another. It might have been in May when I myself got back after being a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said that you went to -- you spent -- you went to Muslim families to celebrate their holiday, Bajram. Do you remember who you spent Bajram with in 1992? What was the name of the family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't celebrate their holidays. I went to visit them as their guest, out of respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I didn't celebrate Bajram. I did visit my friends who celebrated Bajram out of respect for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I understand. I apologise for the misstatement. What friends did you visit in 1992 to visit during -- when they were celebrated Bajram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, I didn't visit anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence you testified that during the -- the spring and summer of 1992, you did not hear any rumours about Milan Lukic being involved in any kind of wrong-doing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you hear any rumours about Sredoje Lukic being involved in any wrong-doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We already have answer in transcript, Your Honour, but just one more time to -- to stress that my client is not mentioned in direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us look at that rule again. What's the Rule, Mr. Groome? Is it 80 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not exactly sure which Rule the Chamber is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it 90 -- 90(h)(i), which says cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief. It's on that basis, Mr. Cepic, that you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is, How is that to be interpreted? I've always found it to be a little limiting myself. Does it mean literally that the cross-examiner cannot mention a name if that name wasn't mentioned in the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it doesn't, and if I would just read the second part of the sentence: "The cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence-in-chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party to the subject matter of that case." Clearly, in this case the witness knows Sredoje Lukic equally well. I should be entitled to put questions with respect to her knowledge of Sredoje Lukic. As well, Mr. Cepic will certainly have an opportunity to ask any other questions of the witness related to those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the part of the Rule that you say allows you to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second part of the sentence in (h)(i), after the comma where it says: "... and, where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party." So in this particular case, it would be where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I don't have that view as Mr. Groome has. I think that this role is clear related to that issue, and also, Mr. Groome quoted that this witness knows Sredoje Lukic equally well, but I did not hear that, and -- but just to conclude this discussion related to Sredoje Lukic, we received from this witness clear answer related to the last question of Mr. Groome. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you assist us in the interpretation of this Rule? I know that in the country where I'm from, the question would be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's up to the discretion of the Court, and beyond the scope of direct examination I understand Mr. Cepic's objection, and we did not bring up Mr. Sredoje Lukic at all in our -- in our direct exam. So I would simply leave it to the discretion of the Court. I think it's -- it's interpretable either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I'm rethinking the interpretation of this, and I'm inclined to believe it must be given the wider -- the wider scope, the broader scope. I can't see how you would be prejudiced because you will have the right to examine on anything raised by Mr. Groome. I'm going to allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just if I may say with your leave, when Mr. Vasiljevic testified before this Honourable Trial Chamber, I requested leave to ask him couple questions on the basis of this -- of the same Rule, and it was not allowed in that situation, but thank you very much for explanation, and if I feel any need, I will ask for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, the next question I'd like to ask you is prior to the war, how would you have characterized the ethnic make-up of the neighborhood you lived in, the Kalate area, mixed ethnicity or predominantly populated by one of the ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us the mix using percentages? Are you able to give us a rough estimate of how mixed it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right bank of the Drina was for the most part Serbian, but there were Muslim houses here and there, while on the left bank there was a purely Muslim population. We accepted them on our side of the river, but they did not accept us on theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you be able to tell me today, just confined to your neighbourhood, Kalate, what would be -- what would be the number of Muslim families that live there today?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object that he's misstating the testimony. She's indicated that she no longer lives in Kalate, so to call it her neighbourhood is a bit misleading, I think. She might be able to figure out what he means by that, but the question as stated is misleading and misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us today the ethnic composition of Kalate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there were some houses there that had been destroyed and that have been rebuilt, but believe me, I have no idea who lives there now because I don't live there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you, how did you come to be a witness in this case? Who asked you to be a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the lawyer who -- who asked you to be a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jelena.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how many times did you meet with Jelena prior to today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you meet with any other members of the Defence team prior to coming here to testify, prior to testifying today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you met with Jelena, did she interview you with respect to what information that you might be able to provide that was relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She asked me whether I wished to testify. I said I did. I would say everything I knew. There was no problem. I asked, What is this about? She said, We will inform you. I signed a statement concerning that woman who was burnt and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the statement that you signed? How -- how long was the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six lines perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have to go anywhere to sign it in terms -- did you go to sign it in front of anyone, or did you just sign it in front of Jelena?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, we had it certified in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In what court did you certify this written statement that you provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the court in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as best you can recall, when was that that you certified this written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- I was experiencing great problems at the time. I was selling my flat in Cacak, and I had to travel a lot, so it's all mixed up as regards the time, but I think it was most probably in October. I'm not a hundred per cent certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I do have the statement at home. I didn't pay attention to the date. I didn't think it was important. Why is it so important?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And have you seen a copy of the statement after arriving here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left that statement at home in Visegrad. I didn't even bring it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it became important, would you be able to provide that statement to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you everything. I've said everything, even more extensively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor took 50 minutes -- I'm sorry, the Defence took 50 minutes, and I'll give you about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, can you see either of the bridges in Visegrad from where you live, where you live at in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see both bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during June -- let's say May to August of 1992, did you ever see anything which you thought was unusual occur on either of the bridges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this period of time, did you travel into town to -- to shop for your family and take care of other -- other chores of daily life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to town every day because I worked in the town, but there was no shopping because there was nothing to be bought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, during your daily excursions into town for work, did you see anything that you thought was unusual occurring in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most often we women talked a lot about the fact that all our husbands, brothers, and friends were in the army. When an action was being prepared, when there was shelling, we only discussed where we would run to and where we would shelter our children. That was a huge problem for us, the biggest problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And aside from that, did you see any other unusual occurrences in the town? People in the town that you had not seen before, armed groups moving through the town, did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were always armed groups in town. It was all our army, police. It was unusual that every day there were funerals. We went to the cemetery every day. Sometimes we had to run because shells landed on the cemetery next to the church. All this was unusual for us. Maybe someone would not find it unusual, but we all found it extremely unusual. I don't know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you more specifically. Do you have any observations about how the Muslim population of Visegrad was treated between June 1992 till about August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Uzice Corps left Visegrad, an offer was made to the Muslims, and I even had occasion several times to see buses. On the radio they called upon them. They said whoever wants to leave Visegrad, transport will be provided. The buses were parked in front of the hotel, and they drove them to wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did those people who got on those buses and leave the town, did they abandon their homes and their farms and their businesses when they did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't take their houses and their land on the bus. When I fled from Visegrad, all I took with me were diapers, Pampers diapers for my children. I couldn't take my home with me. The question is absurd. How can they put their home on a bus and go?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You testified that your husband wore a military uniform during this time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your husband have military duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband had no military duties. Before the war, he didn't even serve in the army because of an injury to his eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who required him to wear a military uniform during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one required anyone to do that, but all the men wore uniforms because they were conscripted, each doing his own job. When they called him up in the Medical Corps to go to the woods because there were wounded there, he wouldn't go there in a white coat and white trousers. It was all camouflaged so that he wouldn't be seen and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's traditional that doctors serving in a military wear a red cross so that they're simply identified as simply being medical personnel. Do you ever recall seeing your husband wearing the red cross on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not wear a red cross, but his paramedic who accompanied him wore a red cross on his arm band, and there were red crosses on the vehicle, just as in the case of UN soldiers. Their doctors also walked around in camouflage uniforms in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. With respect to the information you're providing about Zehra Turjacanin, all of that or the sole source of that is your husband; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only source was he, the book, and what I read here on the internet from The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But with respect to this portion of your evidence with respect to her burning herself on a gas stove, am I correct in thinking that your husband is the sole source of that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He and the sister who with him, accompanying him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's Ms. Papic. Did you speak with Ms. Papic about this as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. She's a nurse, and she no longer lives in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know where she lives today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in Belgrade. I don't know where exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But she didn't tell you about the gas stove. It's simply your husband, Dr. Vasiljevic, who told you about the -- the accident with the gas stove; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on their way back from work together. Her mother's house is a stone's throw from ours. They would go to work together and come back home from work together. We had coffee together every day. We Serbs tend to hang out together a lot, and this is something that I've been telling you about. I think she was there, too, when we were talking about this because they were shocked what the degree of the woman's burns was, how large the burns were, and this was something that a doctor would have found striking. This is not something that you come across every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Ms. -- so, Mrs. Vasiljevic, so it's your testimony that not only did your husband tell you about the accident with the gas stove, but also nurse Papic who accompanied him, she also told you about the accident with the gas stove. Is that your evidence? Yes or no, if you're able to answer it either way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was there when he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I take from your testimony that they told you the day it happened or very shortly after they met with Zehra Turjacanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe that evening or perhaps the next time we met. My husband did not exactly come home every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after that initial time that you had this conversation and your husband told you about Zehra Turjacanin, did you ever discuss it with him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we read about her story, the story that was quite unlike what she had told him and what she had said in that book. I might never have remembered her again in my whole life had it not been for her new statement, which was exactly the reverse of what she had said previously. We were entirely shocked. I hadn't even known what the woman's name was, and I don't think he had either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We just weren't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My time is limited, so I would appreciate if you were able to answer my questions in a brief way, it would help me get through my questions, and we can move on to the next witness. Thank you. When did you first read this book that was sent to you from this person in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps 1995, possibly 1996. I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, between the time that your husband first told you about the gas stove accident and the time you read about Zehra Turjacanin in this book, did you and your husband ever discuss Zehra Turjacanin and her treatment again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did say he was surprised she didn't turn up for the check. He had no idea what had become of her. We didn't even know if she was still alive or dead. Later on, we read the book and he said, Oh, thank God for this. He had obviously provided her with sufficient medicine for her to make it. Had he not assisted her medically, she would not have made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said he was surprised she did not turn up for the check. Am I to take from your answer that your husband told you that he had scheduled an appointment for her to be examined and treated again by your husband? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he gave her an appointment or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the record records you as saying that -- let me just see if I can get the exact reference. I'm sorry. Just bear with me for a minute. Now, the record on page 44, line 10, records you as saying: "He did not" -- "He did say he was surprised she didn't turn up for the check." What did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant that the burns were horrendous, at least based on what he told me. People go back to their doctors even for much slighter injuries, and given the extent of her injuries, it was only surprising that she could would not reappear at some point. He had no idea what had become of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you testified just a question before this one that your husband was surprised that she had made it. Am I to take from that that your husband thought that there was a risk of death that this woman faced because of the severity of her burns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably. He had no opportunity at the time to take her to a hospital anywhere, but he gave her sufficient medicine and told her how to use it, but it is very relative, all things considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you told us that your husband died. Can I ask you what year your husband died, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in 2001 your husband actually came to this Tribunal and testified in the case of Mitar Vasiljevic. Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And he actually sat in the very spot now where you are sitting. Your husband, prior to coming to testify, asked for a certificate of safe passage, in other words, a certificate guaranteeing that he would not be arrested during his travel to and from The Hague. Did he tell you why he felt he needed such protection from being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. This is news to me.
